name: Vanishing Point
mostUsedWayIn: Barclay Creek Trail, right before the bridge, fixed lines to the tower
approach: Start at Barclay Lake trailhead (74920 NE Stevens Pass Hwy, Skykomish, WA 98288). Follow the pleasant level main trail for about 20 minutes to a bridge crossing a large creek (~1 mile). Before the bridge, break right into forest around a large boulder, then walk through relatively open forest or along the creek bed until reaching an open boulder field. Continue through the boulder field to reach steep gullies. Ascend a 60–70° forested rib with fixed lines and natural protection. Climb around the right side of a chossy waterfall (exposed scrambling). Continue up the wash to a ramp with hand lines, then ascend approximately 800 feet of mostly roped-up slab via bolted sections and natural features. Total approach time: 2.5–3.5 hours for competent parties.

name: Standard Scramble
mostUsedWayIn: FR-6517 road end and the counterclockwise traverse
approach: Drive the Beckler River Road (FR-65) out of Skykomish and follow it into the FR-6510/FR-6514/FR-6517 spur network (about 10.8 miles of gravel/dirt forest road past the pavement) to road's end, roughly 0.5 mile east of and nearly level with Eagle Rock's summit — this is the trailhead; there is no maintained trail beyond it. From the parking area, leave the road and head west/southwest straight up the hillside cross-country. You break out of brush and into open forest within the first few hundred feet, then continue uphill through timber; after a few hundred yards the trees give way to open talus slopes below the cliff bands on Eagle Rock's northeast side. name: East Ridge Scramble
trailhead: NF-6514-410 spur end (Beckler River road network)
mostUsedWayIn: Spur road end to Klinger Ridge
approach: Grotto Mountain (5,618') sits east of the more famous Baring Mountain, above the South Fork Skykomish River near the Wild Sky Wilderness boundary. The drive-in is variable and should be reconfirmed with the Skykomish Ranger District, but the trailhead itself is the end of FS spur NF-6514-410, off Beckler River Road (FR-65) — roughly 6.5 miles of gravel/dirt FS road from pavement, ending at a small pullout at about 3,480 ft. There is no maintained trail from here; this is an off-trail scramble the entire way (about 2.4 miles/3,900 ft one-way to the 5,618 ft high point, matching the route's 7.7 km round-trip figure). From road's end, the line immediately enters dense huckleberry brush heading toward talus — a brushy, moss-lined streambed just to the side of the huckleberry slope offers noticeably easier (if slick when wet) passage and is the preferred line reported by recent parties. name: Lewis Creek Route
mostUsedWayIn: Barclay Creek and Tailgunner Pass to the hidden ramp
approach: From the Barclay Lake Trailhead (2,200 ft, end of FR-6024), do not take the maintained Barclay Lake Trail; instead walk back down the access road a short distance to an old spur/climbers' path dropping toward Barclay Creek. Ford Barclay Creek — parties describe essentially two back-to-back crossings, rock-hopping over boulders and deadfall (a small mid-channel island splits the ford), the route's main water hazard and genuinely tricky at high early-season flow. name: Gunnshy Peak Standard Route (Barclay Lake Approach)
mostUsedWayIn: Barclay Lake spur road to the east ridge
approach: From Monroe, drive east on US-2 to the town of Baring. Near milepost 41-42, across from a convenience store, turn left (north) onto 635th Place NE. Cross the railroad tracks and continue about 0.3 mile to a junction; keep left on 635th Place NE for another 0.1 mile, where the road becomes Forest Road 6024 (Barclay Creek Road). Continue roughly 3.9-4.3 miles of gravel forest road (watch for potholes and rough patches; AWD/4x4 recommended after wet weather) to the Barclay Lake Trailhead (vault toilet on site, parking for roughly 20 vehicles, Northwest Forest Pass required). From a spur road near the trailhead, follow the spur toward an old fire pit, where a faint, mostly-unmarked climber's path heads east into the forest and begins the ascent proper.

name: Jötnar
mostUsedWayIn: Lake Serene talus to the left side of the buttress
approach: From the Lake Serene Trailhead, hike Trail #1068 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Lake Serene, then traverse talus and huge boulders around the lake toward its south/southeast end below the Middle Peak (Jötunheim) massif. This cirque holds the Norwegian Buttresses, home to big-wall routes like Jötnar, one of the tallest walls in the Lower 48; reaching the base involves further talus and brush travel beyond the lake. Given the technical, multi-day nature of routes here, most parties approach with overnight gear.

name: Hourglass Gully (Winter)
mostUsedWayIn: Lake Serene Trail #1068, south-end saddle, southwest ridge
approach: Start at the Lake Serene Trailhead and follow Trail #1068 about 4 miles and 2,000 ft of gain to Lake Serene, then traverse talus and boulders around the west side of the lake to its south end. From there head east to a saddle and climb the ridge/gully system southwest of it toward Main Peak, the massif's highest and most technical summit (~5,502 ft). Expect roughly 5,500 ft of total elevation gain, thick brush low on the route, and sustained moderate rock climbing higher up; most parties plan for a 15+ hour car-to-car day or an overnight.

name: Main Peak via North Approach
mostUsedWayIn: Lake Serene Trail #1068 to the North Peak north face
approach: Start at the Lake Serene Trailhead (~600 ft) off Mount Index Road and follow the maintained Lake Serene Trail roughly 4.1 miles and about 2,000 ft of gain — passing the Bridal Veil Falls viewpoint spur around mile 1.6 — up to Lake Serene itself (~2,600 ft). At the lake, leave the maintained trail and pick up the unofficial climbers' path that traverses talus and large boulders along the west/south shore toward the base of North Index's imposing face; in early season this crossing goes over avalanche debris and lingering snow/ice piled at the lake's edge. name: Traverse of Mount Index
mostUsedWayIn: Lake Serene Trail #1068 to the North Peak north face
approach: From the Lake Serene Trailhead, follow the maintained Lake Serene Trail #1068 roughly 4 miles and about 2,000 ft of gain to the lake basin. Traverse around the west side of the lake over talus and boulders to its south end, then climb steep brush and a gully system (snow-covered into early summer) toward the base of the North Peak's North Face. The standard North Face Route is a long, moderate alpine rock climb (Grade III, 5.6-5.7) on featured but sometimes rotten rock with significant brush; parties typically climb it car-to-car in a very long day (12-15+ hours) or with a bivy.

name: West Ridge
trailhead: FR-62 road-end (~2,800 ft, off US-2 near Index)
mostUsedWayIn: FR-62 road end to the west ridge
approach: From US Highway 2 near Index, turn onto Forest Road 62 (also called No Name Creek Road / Proctor Creek Road / Cavanaugh Lake Road). Follow FR-62 about 3.4-3.5 miles to the first junction (~1,600-1,650 ft) and bear left. Continue about 1 mile to a second junction (~2,380 ft) and bear left again. Drive roughly another 0.7-1 mile of increasingly rough road to its end (~2,800 ft), where there is a small pullout/parking area. An unmarked, steep, well-trodden gully directly opposite the pullout marks the boot-path trailhead. Note: FR-62 crosses private industrial timberland and its gate at the highway is frequently locked at the owner's discretion — some parties have had to walk or e-bike an additional ~5+ miles and ~2,500 ft of road to reach this trailhead.

name: North Norwegian Buttress
mostUsedWayIn: Lake Serene to the foot of the buttress
approach: From the Lake Serene Trailhead (~600 ft) off Mount Index Road, follow the maintained Lake Serene Trail — roughly 3.6-4.1 miles (accounts vary slightly) and about 2,000 ft of gain, passing the Bridal Veil Falls spur around mile 1.6 and switchbacking up to Lake Serene (~2,600 ft). At the lake, leave the maintained trail for the unofficial climbers' path that traverses talus and large boulders around the west side of the lake; in early summer this crosses avalanche debris and lingering snow/ice at the lake's edge. Continue up talus beneath the imposing north/east face of North Index toward the cirque below the Norwegian Buttresses, then work up through the brushy base of the wall — steepening mossy slabs and brush that some parties rope up for before reaching clean rock on the buttress proper. approach: The standard approach starts at the Phelps Creek Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft), at the end of Forest Road 6211 off the Chiwawa River Road (FR 62) north of Leavenworth. name: South Route
mostUsedWayIn: Holden Village and the Copper Creek boot trail to the Copper Basin bench
approach: Copper Peak has no drivable trailhead — access is via the Lake Chelan ferry from Fields Point/Chelan to Lucerne Landing, then the Holden Village shuttle bus up to Holden Village (~3,300 ft) in the Railroad Creek valley, Glacier Peak Wilderness. From the village, follow the old mine road/Railroad Creek Trail east roughly 0.5 mile and cross Railroad Creek (footbridge or ford, depending on season) to reach a large tailings pile at about 3,320 ft, where the Copper Creek Trail branches off. This climbers'/boot trail climbs steeply for about 0.7 mile up a hillside (partly burned) before entering the Copper Creek drainage, then parallels the creek south for roughly 3 miles, gaining to about 5,600 ft where it crosses a flat, open bench — this is the standard base camp (Copper Basin) used by nearly all parties. name: West Route / Standard Scramble
mostUsedWayIn: Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to Spider Meadow and upper Phelps Basin
approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (elev. ~3,500 ft, at the end of Phelps Creek Road/FR-6211), follow the Phelps Creek Trail (FST 1511) north up the east side of Phelps Creek through old-growth and second-growth forest. The trail crosses several small side streams (reliable water the whole way) and, in years with heavy winter avalanche activity, threads through 'graveyards' of downed timber deposited across the tread by slide paths off the Ten Peak/Chipmunk Creek slopes to the west — expect some minor scrambling over debris and a couple of ankle-to-shin stream fords early season. The trail climbs gently, gaining roughly 1,900 ft over about 6-7 miles to reach Spider Meadow (~5,400 ft), a broad subalpine meadow with good campsites and the last easy, reliable water before the basin. name: East Ridge
trailhead: Trinity Trailhead (end of Chiwawa River Road)
mostUsedWayIn: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to the Chiwawa-Fortress col
approach: From Trinity Trailhead, hike the Chiwawa River Trail (#1550) north along the valley, passing beneath Red Mountain, to around 6,580 ft, then leave the trail to traverse diagonally up toward Chiwawa Mountain's east ridge, descending to the roughly 7,200 ft col between Chiwawa and Fortress (or continuing over Chiwawa's summit first). Some parties instead approach via the Red Mountain Trail and Chiwawa Basin, fording the Chiwawa River. From the col, a loose class 3-4 gully gains the crest of Fortress's East Ridge.

name: Southwest Face
trailhead: Trinity Trailhead (end of Chiwawa River Road)
mostUsedWayIn: Buck Creek Trail #1513 and the Pass No Pass way-trail
approach: From Trinity Trailhead (2,800 ft) at the end of Chiwawa River Road/FR 6200, follow the Buck Creek Trail (#1513) roughly 9-9.5 miles, climbing through forest, an old avalanche debris field (~4,500 ft), and past an unmarked junction with the Pass No Pass way-trail (bears right, ~5,800 ft). Continue up the way-trail to Pass No Pass (~6,400 ft) and the alpine camping benches beyond, from which Fortress's southwest face and south ridge come into view. Note: since 2026, storm damage has closed FR 6200 to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat Campground (about mile 16), adding roughly 7 miles of road-walking each way before even reaching the trailhead.

name: Southwest Slopes
mostUsedWayIn: Phelps Creek to Leroy Basin, then the couloir toward the Maude col
approach: From the Phelps Creek Trailhead (3,500 ft, end of FR 6211 off Chiwawa River Road), start on Phelps Creek Trail #1511. At about a quarter mile the Carne Mountain Trail splits off steeply to the right (skip it); stay on Phelps Creek Trail as it climbs gently through forest along the creek. At 2.6 mi you cross into Glacier Peak Wilderness. Continue to roughly 3.4–3.5 mi, where the trail crosses Leroy Creek (about 4,140 ft) on a log/rock crossing that can run high with snowmelt in early summer — this is the key junction. Immediately after the crossing, leave the maintained trail and turn right (northeast) onto the unmaintained Leroy Creek climbers' trail, which follows the north side of Leroy Creek and gains roughly 2,000 ft in about 1.5 miles of steep, sometimes brushy, boot-track tread — this is the stiffest sustained pitch of the day. name: Standard Scramble (Marmot Lake / O'Neil Pass approach)
approach: From the Duckabush Trailhead (end of Forest Service Road 2510, ~440 ft, reached via US-101 south of Quilcene), follow the Duckabush River Trail #803 upriver. The first ~2.4 miles run at an easy grade along the river through old-growth forest, then the trail climbs steadily and at times steeply (~1,000 ft) to crest Big Hump at about mile 3.9 — the trail's first real obstacle, made looser and more exposed to sun/blowdown by a 2011 human-caused fire that scorched a swath of old growth on the Hump. approach: Start at the Duckabush Trailhead (FR 2510-060) off US 101 and follow the Duckabush River Trail #803. trailhead: Staircase Trailhead (North Fork Skokomish, Olympic NP)

approach: Drive Hwy 101 to Hoodsport, then SR-119 (North Lake Cushman Road, becomes FR-24 past the lake) roughly 9 miles to the Staircase Ranger Station/trailhead (~800 ft) in the SE corner of Olympic National Park. Hike the North Fork Skokomish River Trail ~3.4 miles to the Spike Camp junction, then climb steeply another ~3.6 miles to Flapjack Lakes (~4,000 ft, 8 miles from the trailhead) — a limited-entry wilderness camping zone, so reserve a permit well ahead. From Flapjack Lakes, continue ~1.5 miles up to Gladys Divide (~5,000 ft), then traverse cross-country toward Sawtooth/Needle Pass to reach the base of The Fin and The Horn. Round-trip approach mileage to Gladys Divide alone runs close to 19 miles with roughly 4,000+ ft of net gain, before the additional ridge travel and the climb itself — this is realistically a backpack-in with a high camp, not a day trip from the road.

name: North Slopes from Lake Valhalla
mostUsedWayIn: Smithbrook Trail to Union Gap and the Lake Valhalla crest trail
approach: From US Highway 2 about 4 miles east of Stevens Pass, turn onto Smith Brook Road (Forest Road 6700) and follow the gravel road roughly 2.6-2.8 miles to the Smithbrook Trailhead (el. ~4,000 ft; no fee, no Northwest Forest Pass required). Hike Smithbrook Trail #1590 through old-growth forest, entering the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness at about 0.5 mile, and continue to Union Gap (el. ~4,600-4,688 ft) at roughly 1.0-1.3 miles, where the trail meets the Pacific Crest Trail. Turn south (left) on the PCT for about 1.4 miles through forest with views toward Lichtenberg Mountain and Nason Ridge, to an unnamed gap at about 5,100 ft. Just before/at this gap, an unmarked but obvious boot path breaks off to the north through heather meadows, climbing a steep, sometimes brushy and eroded 0.5 mile (about 650 ft of additional gain) to the true summit.

name: South Slopes Scramble
mostUsedWayIn: Skyline Lake and the boulder garden
approach: From the Stevens Pass Ski Area's north (uphill) lot, walk to the far east end of the parking area near the small gray electrical substation/WSDOT building — this is the unsigned Skyline Lake trailhead. In summer, take the gravel service road on the left side of the substation, passing beneath the powerlines; a steeper, faster boot path also splits off directly across from the WSDOT building for hikers who want to skip the road switchbacks. Follow the road/track uphill, staying left, then bear right shortly after — a vehicle gate blocks the road about a quarter mile up. The road/trail climbs steadily (roughly 500 ft of gain per half-mile in the steepest stretch) through forest and talus for about 1.2-1.3 miles to Skyline Lake (~1,100-1,300 ft gained, lake sits around 4,900-5,100 ft). name: Slippery Slab Tower NE Face
areaName: Thunder Mountain and Slippery Slab Tower
trailhead: Tunnel Creek or Surprise Creek Trailheads (US-2)
mostUsedWayIn: Tunnel Creek trail to the crest trail at the lake, then south to the pass
otherWaysIn: Surprise Creek trail past the two lakes, then the switchbacks to the pass
approach: From either trailhead, climbers first gain the Pacific Crest Trail — via the Tunnel Creek Trail climbing about 1,170 ft in 1.45 miles to Hope Lake, or via the Surprise Creek Trail past Surprise and Glacier Lakes — then follow the PCT south several miles to Trap Pass (~5,800 ft). From Trap Pass an unmaintained climbers' trail continues south along the ridge to the base of Slippery Slab Tower, with Thunder Mountain further along the same ridgeline above Glacier Lake. The round trip is long enough (roughly 10+ miles one-way) that many parties camp overnight at Hope Lake or Trap Lake.

name: Southeast Slopes Scramble
mostUsedWayIn: Smithbrook Trail to Union Gap
approach: Drive US 2 to Smithbrook Road (Forest Road 6700); the turnoff is about 4.2 miles east of Stevens Pass summit (roughly half a mile east of milepost 69 coming from the Leavenworth/Wenatchee side, or about 68 miles from Everett/Seattle). Follow FR 6700 about 2.7-3 miles to the Smithbrook Trailhead (~4,000 ft) on the left; the gravel road is normally passable to passenger cars once it's snow-free but is not plowed in winter, when parking shifts to a highway-side pullout and adds miles of road travel each way. From the trailhead, Smithbrook Trail #1590 climbs about 1 mile to the PCT junction at Union Gap, the start of the scramble route described in Beta.

name: Southwest Slope (Standard Route)
mostUsedWayIn: Devore Creek Trail from Bird Creek Camp over the Enigma saddle
approach: From Chelan, take the Lady of the Lake ferry (or a floatplane) to Stehekin Landing. Ride the NPS shuttle bus 4.4 miles up Stehekin Valley Road to Harlequin Bridge ($5 fare), cross the bridge, and follow the road past Harlequin Camp and the Stehekin Airport to pick up the Stehekin River Trail. Follow this mostly flat trail southeastward about 3 miles to the signed Devore Creek Trail junction. The Devore Creek Trail then climbs steeply through rock bluffs and open forest for about 1 mile, enters the Glacier Peak Wilderness, and traverses brushy, dry hillside for roughly 3 more miles to Bird Creek Camp (4,200 ft) — the only designated camp in the area, with room for about three tents. approach: McGregor Mountain is only reachable via Stehekin, at the head of Lake Chelan, which has no outside road access — get there by the Lady of the Lake ferry, floatplane, or the long trail from Cascade Pass/Bridge Creek. name: Southwest Ridge Route
mostUsedWayIn: Agnes Creek and the Swamp Creek drainage to the west basin
approach: Via passenger ferry or floatplane from Chelan to Stehekin, then the PCT/Stehekin Valley Road to High Bridge; follow the Agnes Creek Trail and Swamp Creek drainage to Lyall's west basin. Roughly 35-40 miles round trip from High Bridge, so most parties camp en route. From the west basin, climb talus and heather to gain the southwest ridge, passing below a distinctive band of white rock; the route narrows into an exposed Class 3 gully near the summit, finishing over stacked Class 3-4 boulders to the summit block.

At about 0.3 mi bear toward Sunrise Point/Klahhane Ridge Trail and continue along open, exposed subalpine ridge (alternating meadow and pocket forest) for roughly 2.5 mi to an unsigned junction where a distinct, unmaintained 'climbers trail' splits left (west) off the maintained Klahhane Ridge Trail — this is the start of the true scramble route (sometimes mapped as the Mount Angeles Summit Climbers Trail). A shorter, steeper alternative start exists directly off Hurricane Ridge Road at the Switchback Trail (~mile marker in the last few miles before the visitor center), which gains about 700-800 ft in 0.6 mi to meet the Mount Angeles Trail higher up, cutting off some of the ridge walk. name: Standard Route (Carrie Glacier / High Divide)

approach: From US-101 about 2 miles west of Lake Crescent, turn onto Sol Duc Hot Springs Road and drive roughly 14 miles past Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort to the road-end trailhead (Sol Duc River Trailhead, ~2,000 ft). Hike the Sol Duc River Trail past Sol Duc Falls, continue about 1 mile past the Deer Lake Trail junction, then roughly 6 more miles to Heart Lake (4,800 ft). From Heart Lake, climb 1.5 miles to the High Divide crest (~5,100 ft) and follow High Divide south/west about 3 miles to where the maintained trail ends near Bogachiel Peak. approach: There is no trail to Mount Fairchild itself, but the standard approach follows a well-defined maintained-trail corridor before turning to off-trail wilderness travel. Start at the Sol Duc River Trailhead (end of Sol Duc Road) on the Sol Duc River Trail. name: Bailey Range Scramble
trailhead: Hoh River Trailhead (Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center)
mostUsedWayIn: Hoh River and the Blue Glacier to Glacier Pass
approach: Drive the paved Upper Hoh Road to its end at the Hoh Ranger Station (578 ft). Hike the Hoh River Trail 17.2 miles to Glacier Meadows (~4,200-4,300 ft), the standard base camp for this side of the range (note: a washed-out section partway up requires a fixed ladder/rope crossing). From Glacier Meadows, follow the way trail 0.8 mi to the top of the Blue Glacier lateral moraine, continue along the moraine crest ~0.2 mi, then descend onto the Blue Glacier and ascend snow slopes around rock islands to the crest of Snow Dome (6,600 ft). From Snow Dome, rope up and traverse the upper Hoh Glacier toward Glacier Pass (between Mathias and the East Peak of Olympus), then gain the base of either the Mathias snow finger or the steep gullies leading to the Mercury-Mathias col.

name: Ruth Peak Scramble
mostUsedWayIn: High Divide and the Catwalk to Eleven Bull Basin
approach: From the Sol Duc Trailhead (~1,900 ft), follow the Sol Duc River Trail through old-growth forest to Sol Duc Park, then climb to Heart Lake (7.85 mi) and the High Divide/Bailey Range junction (~8.3 mi, ~5,050 ft). Leave the maintained trail here and drop off the High Divide via the boot-path known as the 'Catwalk' (class 2-3 scrambling that can hold snow into midsummer), passing below Cat Peak and Stephen Peak. Continue cross-country toward Eleven Bull Basin, a meadow on Ruth Peak's south flank with reliable water and established tent pads on the knob above the basin — roughly 15 mi and ~6,000 ft of cumulative gain from the trailhead. From camp, scramble class 2-3 talus/scree north to the summit.

mostUsedWayIn: Butte Pass, Pass Butte and the connecting ridge
approach: Lost Peak sits deep in the Pasayten Wilderness and the standard approach is a serious backcountry undertaking, not a day hike from a roadside trailhead. From the Monument Creek Trailhead (2,400 ft, off Lost River Road) follow Monument Creek Trail #484, which is well-maintained through old-growth forest for the first ~4 miles along Monument Creek and the Lost River — water is plentiful here and this stretch is even rideable by mountain bike, which some parties use to bank easy miles before caching bikes at the wilderness boundary. name: South Slopes Scramble
trailhead: Monument Creek Trailhead (Lost River Road / Harts Pass Road)
mostUsedWayIn: The south gully below the Carru-Lago col
approach: Two standard approaches leave from the Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) area near Slate Peak (~6,900-7,400 ft, one of the highest drivable roads in Washington): (1) the shortest line drops from Slate Pass/Buckskin Ridge down the West/Middle Fork Pasayten River to Fred's Lake/Fred's Pass, then crosses upper Eureka Creek toward Shellrock Basin below the Carru-Lago-Osceola cirque — about 15 miles one-way; (2) the Monument Creek Trail, also off Harts Pass Road, is roughly 19 miles one-way with more up-and-down elevation change. Pasayten trails are lightly maintained — expect blowdown on the Middle Fork Pasayten Trail and stretches where the tread is fainter than GPS basemaps suggest, so off-trail navigation skill is required.

name: South Slope - South Face (Standard Route)
trailhead: Robinson Creek Trailhead (Lost River Road / Forest Road 5400)
mostUsedWayIn: Shellrock Basin and the Lago-Carru col
approach: From the Robinson Creek Trailhead (~2,500 ft, via SR-20 and Lost River Road/Forest Road 5400 west of Winthrop) or the higher Slate Peak Trailhead (~7,170 ft, via the Hart's Pass spur road), follow the Robinson Creek/Middle Fork Pasayten Trail over Robinson Pass and down into the Middle Fork Pasayten drainage. Continue north past the Eureka Creek Trail junction (~5,190 ft) to Fred's Lake (6,507 ft), a common camp and water source below Lago's west side. From Fred's Lake, follow the unmaintained middle section of the Eureka Creek Trail (or cross-country) east across the upper Eureka Creek basin - the creek crossing can be difficult when swollen with snowmelt - to reach Shellrock Basin/Shellrock Pass on the south side of the Lago-Carru ridge. The shortest road-based approach is roughly 16 miles one-way, typically covered over 1-2 days.

name: Austera Peak
trailhead: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
mostUsedWayIn: Eldorado camp, Klawatti Col, and the 75-ft rappel onto the Klawatti Glacier
approach: From Seattle, drive I-5 north and then WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) east through Sedro-Woolley, Concrete, and Rockport to Marblemount, then follow Cascade River Road south for about 20 miles — paved for the first 10 miles, gravel and washboard the rest of the way — to the Eldorado parking area near mile 20. name: East Ridge / Inspiration Glacier
trailhead: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
mostUsedWayIn: Inspiration and McAllister to the col between Point 8386 and the Needle
approach: Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount about 20 miles to the Eldorado Trailhead (~2,100 ft; first 10 miles paved, remainder rough gravel, high-clearance recommended). Hike the Eldorado Trail through forest, cross a creek, and climb steeply to the Eldorado Glacier, then follow the East Ridge of Eldorado Peak to a high camp around 7,400 ft (roughly 4 miles and ~6,000 ft of gain). From camp, rope up and traverse the Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier to reach the col at the base of Dorado Needle's East Ridge.

The unmaintained boot path climbs through forest and then talus (roughly 1,500 ft of gain) before breaking into open slopes; stay right of the large windfall area and avoid crossing Eldorado Creek. name: Southwest Buttress

approach: The hike-in to the Southwest Buttress follows the identical trailhead-to-glacier approach as the East Ridge: from the Eldorado Trailhead on Cascade River Road, cross the Cascade River/Eldorado Creek near the parking area (backtrack downstream to find a log or ford), pick up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek, and climb steeply through old-growth forest (no water on this stretch) to a talus field around 4,000 ft. Re-cross Eldorado Creek near a cairn at about 5,100 ft, switchback up past 6,000 ft, and drop via a short Class 3 gully into Roush Creek basin (6,100-6,400 ft, reliable water, a good lower camp/bail-out point). From the basin, ascend 20-30-degree snow onto the toe of the Eldorado Glacier at about 7,500 ft - rope up for crevasse hazard from here on - and establish a high camp on rock/moraine near the glacier shoulder for the multi-day stay. name: North Ridge
mostUsedWayIn: One col further: Klawatti Col to the Klawatti-Austera col, then the crest
approach: From Marblemount on WA-20, drive the Cascade River Road (FR-15) about 19-21 miles (paved to roughly mile 10, then gravel/washboard) to the Eldorado trailhead (~2,150 ft). Cross the North Fork Cascade River and follow the unmaintained Eldorado climbers' trail through forest and a boulder field to treeline, then to Eldorado Basin/Roush Creek camps (~6,000-6,300 ft). Ascend the Eldorado Glacier snow dome to the ~7,500-ft notch on Eldorado's lower East Ridge, traverse ~1.5 miles north across the upper Inspiration Glacier to Klawatti Col (7,800 ft), then continue easily to the nearby Klawatti-Austera Col (7,900 ft) to start the ridge.

name: Southeast Buttress
mostUsedWayIn: Andrews Creek trail #504 from the Chewuch River road
otherWaysIn: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee
approach: Drive to the Andrews Creek Trailhead (~3,050 ft) at the end of West Chewuch Road/FR-51, roughly 22–23.5 miles north of Winthrop. From the trailhead, follow Andrews Creek Trail #504, which climbs steadily through the Andrews Creek drainage — the first ~6-12 miles pass through the 2003 wildfire burn scar, so expect little shade, brushy/overgrown tread in early season (some parties describe being soaked to the skin pushing through wet regrowth after rain), and occasional blowdowns despite periodic trail-crew clearing. Andrews Creek itself parallels the trail for this stretch and is a reliable water source. At about 12 miles the trail tops out at Andrews Pass (6,680+ ft), where the burn gives way to open parkland and meadow with views north toward Amphitheater Mountain; snow patches can linger here into early July. camps.notes: The standard planned high camp, in an open meadow basin at the treeline with the glacier toe above. It is a pleasant place — flowers, waterfalls, and correspondingly aggressive marmots and bugs — but earning it means a long approach and then a steep, unmaintained climbers' path straight up a foreste

camps.name: Sitkum Creek / PCT junction camp
camps.notes: A lower fallback for parties who run out of daylight on the long walk in, sitting where the climbers' path leaves the maintained trail. Below treeline, so it is sheltered and out of the weather, but it leaves the entire steep climbers' path plus 1,500 ft of gain before you are even at the standard c

camps.name: Kennedy Guard Station area
camps.notes: The lowest planned stop, about 5.5 miles in and still widely used. Do not plan on soaking: the historic hot pool, lodge and guard station here were buried by the 2003 flood and debris flow and were never rebuilt. Useful as a first night for parties splitting the approach, or as a retreat in bad weat

name: Southeast Slopes
mostUsedWayIn: Access Creek basin, then the gap south of Point 6,730 and the 6,600 ft basin traverse to Luna Col
approach: The trip starts at the Ross Dam Trailhead on SR 20 (North Cascades Highway, ~2,050ft), where parking is right off the highway. From there it's about a 0.8-mile hike down the Ross Dam Trail to Ross Lake, then a boat shuttle (Ross Lake Resort water taxi, or a paddled canoe/packraft for parties without a shuttle reservation) roughly 9 miles up-lake to the Big Beaver Trailhead (~1,600ft) near the Big Beaver / 39 Mile camp area — this lake crossing is a key logistical step, not an afterthought, since Ross Lake Resort's shuttle season and hours govern when you can actually reach the trailhead. From the Big Beaver Trailhead, follow the Big Beaver Trail through old-growth cedar forest along the north bank of Big Beaver Creek for about 8 miles to Luna Camp (an established backcountry campsite, permit required from the NPS backcountry office), gaining only modest elevation on generally mellow, wel

camps.name: Luna Camp (Big Beaver Trail)
camps.notes: The signed camp about 8 miles up the Big Beaver Trail from the boat landing, in old-growth cedar and only modestly above lake level. It is a trail camp, not a mountain one, and it earns its place because the water-taxi timetable often puts you on the trail late. From here it is another 1.5 miles nor

camps.name: Access Creek headwaters basin
camps.notes: The open basin at the top of the Access Creek approach, roughly 1,700 ft above Luna Camp and the standard base for the peak. Getting here is the hard part: valley-bottom devil's club, a crossing to the north bank, then a swap back to the south side near 3,700-3,800 ft where cairns and a faint path u

name: Eel Glacier / Flypaper Pass
mostUsedWayIn: Dosewallips road walk, West Fork to Anderson Pass and the tarn camp
otherWaysIn: East Fork Quinault and Enchanted Valley to Anderson Pass from the west
approach: From US-101 at Brinnon, turn onto Dosewallips Road and drive roughly 5.5 miles to the washed-out gate — the road has been closed to vehicles since a 2002 flood and remains closed indefinitely as of recent seasons; park here (a mountain bike is a real time-saver for the road-walk ahead). Follow the bypass trail around the washout — a short ~0.3-mile detour with a few switchbacks past old-growth trees — then rejoin the abandoned roadbed and continue roughly 5.6 more miles to the Dosewallips Ranger Station (1,600 ft). From the ranger station, pick up the Dosewallips River Trail for 1.4 miles to its junction with the West Fork Dosewallips Trail (Trail #1010); bear onto the West Fork Trail and follow the river upstream past a string of established camps — Dose Forks, Big Timber, Diamond Meadows — to Honeymoon Meadows (3,527 ft, about 8 trail-miles from the ranger station). Expect at least one

camps.name: Honeymoon Meadows
camps.notes: PLANNED camp and the last big established site on the West Fork, roughly eight trail-miles past the ranger station. Dry ground at the far end of the meadows once the snow goes. Getting here involves at least one calf- to knee-deep ford of the West Fork depending on melt, so arrive with time to deal

camps.name: Camp Siberia / Anderson Pass shelter area
camps.notes: PLANNED alternative about 0.7 mile and 700 ft above Honeymoon Meadows, below Anderson Pass. Sheltered and in trees, which is its value in weather — but parties routinely walk past it without finding it under snow, so do not commit to it as your only plan on a late arrival. It is still below the pass

camps.name: Tarn camp above Anderson Pass
camps.notes: PLANNED high camp and the one worth reaching — open slopes above Anderson/Valkyrie Lake, roughly a mile past the pass up the climbers' path and moraine, and preferred by parties specifically to avoid sleeping in the forest at or below the pass. Budget 7-9 hours from the road closure to here. This is

name: North Chimney (Standard Route)
mostUsedWayIn: Dosewallips roadbed, Lake Constance trail, Avalanche Canyon and the South Chute
otherWaysIn: Bike the closed Dosewallips roadbed
approach: Park at the Dosewallips Road washout (~600 ft), reached via ~7 paved miles then ~3 gravel miles of FR 2610 from US 101 at Brinnon (closed to vehicles since a 2002 washout). From the gate, walk or mountain-bike the old roadbed roughly 5-6 more miles up the Dosewallips valley to the signed, unmaintained Lake Constance climbers' path (no official Forest Service trail number — this is a boot path, not a maintained trail). The path launches almost immediately into sustained, root-and-log 'veggie belay' climbing through old burn debris for the first ~0.4 mile before old-growth forest closes in. At about 0.8 mile you pass Half Acre Rock, a large monolith with established campsites and a common water/rest stop on Constance Creek, which parallels the lower trail (by late summer the creek and canyon above run dry, so treat this as your last reliable water before the lake). camps.name: Lake Constance
camps.notes: The only practical camp for the route and a brutal one to reach: an unmaintained climbers' path gaining roughly 3,200 ft in about 1.8 mi from the Dosewallips, steep enough that you are pulling on roots and logs, and that is after walking or biking several miles of the road washed out since 2002. Par

name: Southeast Glaciers (Standard)
mostUsedWayIn: Ross Lake water taxi, Big Beaver Creek Trail, the Access Creek bushwhack, Access Col and Luna Pass
approach: From the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR 20 (~milepost 134, 2,150 ft), it's about 1 mile down to the Ross Lake water taxi dock; cross the lake by taxi (or paddle) to Big Beaver Landing. From the landing, follow the Big Beaver Creek Trail 11.5 miles up-valley — a dry, well-maintained, largely flat trail taking roughly 5 hours, passing Luna Camp around the 4.7-hour mark. About 29 minutes beyond Luna Camp, a large (~15-inch-diameter) log crossing of Big Beaver Creek marks the turnoff: leave the trail here and head up the Access Creek drainage. This next mile is a real bushwhack, gaining roughly 1,900 ft (2,400 ft to 4,300 ft): start in valley-bottom devil's club, cross to the creek's north side around 3,800 ft where brush pinches in on both banks, then climb through moderately dense huckleberry brush before the final half-mile of talus into Access Basin — watch for deadfall, thick u

camps.name: Luna Col (Luna Pass)
camps.notes: The standard high camp and the base for summit day on Fury, reached after a long steep heather-and-talus traverse from Access Col. camps.name: Access Basin camp
camps.notes: A planned camp used to break the approach, at the head of Access Creek where the bushwhack finally opens onto talus. It is the last water before the long, hot, shadeless scree chute up to Access Col, and it is where most parties stash anything not needed above. It is not scenic or comfortable — brus

name: Stujack Pass + Summit Scramble
mostUsedWayIn: Mt. Pugh Trail #644 from FR-2095 to Stujack Pass
approach: From I-5 exit 208, drive east on SR-530 through Arlington and continue about 28 miles to Darrington. At the four-way stop in town, turn right (south) onto the Mountain Loop Highway and follow it roughly 14 miles — paved, then graveled — to FR-2095 (the Mt. Pugh Spur Road), signed with a large prominent marker on the left. Turn left onto FR-2095 and continue about 1 mile to the Mt. Pugh Trailhead (#644) on the right; parking at the trailhead itself is very limited (a handful of cars), so the large pullout at the switchback just below the trailhead is a reliable overflow option. From the trailhead, Trail #644 climbs through deep old-growth forest with several stream crossings, gaining about 1,300 ft over 1.5 miles to Lake Metan, a small subalpine tarn that serves as the natural 'base' before the ascent steepens toward Stujack Pass.

camps.name: Mount Pugh road end, Forest Road 2095
camps.notes: The staging point for MOUNT PUGH, which most parties climb in a single long day from here — around five and a half miles and well over five thousand feet to the summit, with the character changing three times on the way. Forest and stream crossings to the lake at a mile and a half, then a steady cli

camps.name: Lake Metan, Mount Pugh trail
camps.notes: A mile and a half and about thirteen hundred feet up from the road end, on a short signed spur off the main trail, this is the only established camping on the Pugh approach and it turns a punishing day into a manageable one. Its real value is for a party that wants the ridge above Stujack Pass in th

camps.name: Stujack Pass and the benches just below it
camps.notes: This is a high bivouac rather than a camp, and it exists for one purpose — putting a party on the exposed upper ridge of MOUNT PUGH at first light rather than in the afternoon, when the scrambling section around the head of the small glacier is more pleasant and the weather is more predictable. From

name: Sunset Ridge
mostUsedWayIn: Westside Road, Round Pass, St Andrews Park and the Puyallup Cleaver
approach: From the Westside Road gate (~2,900 ft, about a mile past the Nisqually entrance), walk the road roughly 3.5 miles to Round Pass, then follow the South Puyallup River Trail to the Wonderland Trail and on to Saint Andrews Park. Leave the trail and climb north through alpine meadows to the Puyallup Cleaver (passing Tokaloo Spire), then leave the cleaver at about 8,500 ft to traverse the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers into the Sunset Amphitheater.

camps.name: Colonnade Ridge
camps.notes: PLANNED camp, the first reasonable stopping point once you leave the Wonderland Trail and start up toward the Puyallup Cleaver. It is a snow camp, so it depends entirely on coverage — in a dry year the ground here is bare and the site is much less pleasant. Parties who stop here accept a very long s

camps.name: Puyallup Cleaver high camp
camps.notes: PLANNED camp and the usual high camp for the route, on the cleaver at roughly this height before it is left at about 8,500 ft for the glacier traverse. Mixed snow and rock, wind-exposed on a west-facing rib with nothing upwind of it. Site on the cleaver crest rather than in a runnel, and keep clear

camps.name: Open bivouac near 9,600 ft
camps.notes: PLANNED but committing — used specifically to cut the summit day down, and on record as an open bivouac rather than a sheltered site. There is nothing here but what you dig. In a dry season the transition from this height onto the face is the part that turns parties around, so the higher camp only p

camps.name: Bergschrund camp in the Sunset Amphitheater
camps.notes: PLANNED camp reached by leaving the cleaver near 8,500 ft, traversing the Puyallup and South Mowich glaciers and climbing a steep snow gully to a small bergschrund with good ground beside it. The caution is the amphitheater itself: the headwall above sheds ice and rock, so this only makes sense site

name: Standard Scramble
mostUsedWayIn: Olney Creek Road gate, the closed logging road and One Acre Lake
approach: From the gate on Olney Creek Road (the drive-in ends here, at roughly 2,100 ft, since the road has been closed to public vehicle travel), the route starts as a road-walk. Follow the closed logging road uphill for about 2.25 miles, past a first switchback and on to a second switchback where the grade eases around 3,700 ft — this is the key junction. Leave the road here and pick up an unsigned but well-established climbers' path on the right (north) side, which climbs onto and follows a forest ridge crest. The path fades out around 4,050-4,200 ft; from that point, leave any tread and traverse southeast cross-country, aiming for a small pond just northeast of point 4875, then continue southeast to a second minor ridge. Cross open slopes on this ridge into the rocky basin holding One Acre Lake (roughly 6 miles and ~3,000 ft of gain from the road gate/Sultan Basin Road) — this is the last rel

camps.name: San Juan Campground, Index-Galena road
camps.notes: The nearest developed camp to the Spire Mountain roadhead, sitting on the Index-Galena road a few miles below where the climb starts. It spent close to two decades unreachable by vehicle after flood damage took out the road, and access has been restored and lost again more than once since; treat its

camps.name: One Acre Lake, under Mount Stickney
camps.notes: The one place worth camping on Mount Stickney, and the reason the peak is doable at all now that the road is gated low. The route leaves the Sultan Basin road onto the old Olney Creek logging road, which used to let a high-clearance vehicle grind up to around 2,100 feet and is now closed at its very

camps.name: Sultan Basin road pullouts and the Olney Creek gate
camps.notes: A pure staging pullout for Mount Stickney, included because the road walk is now long enough that starting it at first light matters. name: Northwest Couloir (Cedar Creek approach)
approach: From Highway 20 near Winthrop, reach the Cedar Creek Trailhead (reported at 2,961 ft elevation) and follow the Cedar Creek Trail before leaving it to bushwhack cross-country toward Cedar Creek; a known ford crossing (via a log in some years, a wade in others) gives access to the Shelokum Creek drainage, which is followed trail-less uphill to open meadows/snowfields below the northwest couloir.

camps.name: Klipchuck Campground and the Highway 20 road-head campgrounds
camps.notes: The obvious place to sleep before starting up either side of the Gardners, and the only one with running water and a toilet. It sits in ponderosa forest just off the highway about four miles beyond Mazama, and the Cedar Creek trailhead is roughly half a mile further along a short forest road — near

camps.name: Cedar Creek meadow camps above the falls
camps.notes: The western approach camp, and the reason to use this side at all. Cedar Falls comes at about 1.7 miles from the trailhead and is the day-hike turnaround for most visitors; keep going and roughly two miles beyond the falls the trail opens into meadows with good camping. From here the head of the val

camps.name: Upper Cedar Creek head basin
camps.notes: A spring and early-summer bivouac rather than a camp, used by parties taking the west side of North Gardner when snow still covers the ground. Getting into the head of the valley involves leaving the maintained trail and working up through brush, and it is not pleasant in dry conditions — the argume

name: Sahale Arm / Sahale Glacier
mostUsedWayIn: Cascade Pass Trail and Sahale Arm to Sahale Glacier Camp
otherWaysIn: Car-to-car day push
approach: From the Cascade Pass Trailhead (3,600 ft) at the end of Cascade River Road, follow the Cascade Pass Trail through old-growth timber via roughly 35 well-graded switchbacks, gaining about 1,800 ft in the first 2 miles before the grade eases through subalpine meadows to Cascade Pass (5,400 ft) at about 3.5-3.7 miles. At the pass, take the left (north) fork signed for Sahale Arm and switchback up the open, increasingly rocky ridge crest - the Sahale Arm Trail, about 2.1-2.2 miles and 2,200 ft of additional gain, with views down to Doubtful Lake (a worthwhile ~1-mile, 1,000-ft side trip on a signed spur if you want water or to scout the basin) and across to Johannesburg Mountain, Magic Mountain, and Mixup Peak. The maintained trail ends around 7,200-7,600 ft at Sahale Glacier Camp, a cluster of rock-walled tent pads that also serves as the NPS-permitted high camp (wilderness permit required,

camps.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
camps.notes: A planned camp and one of the highest in the park, where the maintained trail ends: flat gravel tent pads built onto rock mounds at the foot of the glacier, each ringed by a primitive dry-stone wall, plus a composting toilet. Those walls are there because the site is completely exposed to wind and w

camps.name: Doubtful Lake
camps.notes: The lower fallback, roughly a mile and a thousand feet down a signed spur off the arm. It has water when the high camp does not and it is far more sheltered in bad weather, at the cost of re-gaining that thousand feet to rejoin the route. Worth knowing because there is no camping permitted anywhere

name: South Couloir (Standard Route)
mostUsedWayIn: Early-season snow ascent
otherWaysIn: Lena Lake and the Brothers climbers' path (summer)
approach: From the Lena Lake Trailhead (Trail #810) off FS-25 at roughly 700 ft, hike the maintained Lena Lake Trail about 3 miles and ~1,100 ft of gain through second-growth and old-growth forest, crossing several creek drainages on the way, to Lena Lake (~1,800 ft) — a popular backpacking destination with a ranger station and established campsites, and the last easy, reliable water/camping before the climbers' route. Skirt the west side of the lake and pick up the unmaintained but well-trodden 'Brothers Trail' boot path, which continues up the East Fork Lena Creek drainage through the old-growth 'Valley of the Silent Men' for roughly another 2.5-3 miles to a climbers' camp (sometimes called Camp Brothers) at about 2,900 ft, marked by a fire ring — most parties treat this as their high camp for a two-day ascent. From camp, leave the tread and follow a climbers' path along the west fork of Lena Cr

camps.name: Lower Lena Lake
camps.notes: Three miles in, and worth knowing about mainly so you do not mistake it for the climb's camp — it is a further three miles and about a thousand feet below the ground climbers actually use. It suits a party arriving late in the day or a first night split, not a summit bid.

camps.name: Brothers base camp at Lena Forks
camps.notes: The base camp for the route, at the confluence of the forks of the East Fork of Lena Creek, roughly five to six miles in and about three miles beyond the north end of Lena Lake. camps.name: Upper camp above the forks
camps.notes: A second camp area further up the basin, reached by following the cairned way trail toward the left fork until a small meadow opens.
